# Incident Report: Host Compromise via Information-Stealing Malware
**Evidence:** `2022-01-07-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (SHA256: `a86b11ee443ee59d95e4590bdf761235c5d240128d6d195233d065ab57777e8b`), 5,880 frames, 750.8 sec duration, capture starting 2022-01-07 20:04:09 (local capture time). No IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived entirely from packet-level analysis (tshark).

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 192.168.1.216 |
| MAC address | 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9 (ASUSTek NIC) |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 (confirmed via DHCP option 12, Kerberos CNameString, mDNS, LLMNR, and NTLM auth hostname) |
| AD domain | SPOONWATCH (DC: SPOONWATCH-DC.spoonwatch.net, 192.168.1.2) |
| Logged-in user | steve.smith (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ CNameString and SMB2/NTLM auth against the DC, domain SPOONWATCH) |

## 2. Malware Family

**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no AV/IDS alert files were provided in the evidence set; classification is based on the distinctive traffic pattern below).

The traffic matches the known behavioral profile of the **Vidar Stealer** family (an Arkei/Mars-lineage information stealer):

- At 20:07:32, `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2` opened a single plaintext HTTP connection (TCP stream 65) directly to an IP address with **no preceding DNS lookup** — consistent with a hardcoded/config-embedded C2 address, a common stealer evasion trait.
- It issued 7 sequential `POST` requests disguised as image downloads (`/osk//6.jpg`, `/osk//1.jpg`, `/osk//2.jpg`, `/osk//3.jpg`, `/osk//4.jpg`, `/osk//5.jpg`, `/osk//7.jpg`), each returning `Content-Type: image/jpeg` but actually delivering **PE32 DLLs** (`MZ`/`PE` headers confirmed in every payload). String analysis of the recovered binaries identifies them as the classic Mozilla/Visual-C++ runtime bundle used by stealers to read and decrypt browser credential stores: `sqlite3.dll`, `nss3.dll`, `freebl3.dll`, `softokn3.dll`, `nssdbm3.dll`, `msvcp140.dll`/`vcruntime140.dll`.
- It then checked in with `POST /osk//main.php` (200 OK, empty body).
- It finished with a single large `POST /osk/` (Content-Length: 379,629 bytes) — the exfiltration. The uploaded multipart body's internal filenames confirm a stealer-style loot archive: `Content-Disposition: filename="_5861695120.zip"` containing `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `autofill/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, and `system.txt` — i.e., stolen browser autofill data, saved credit-card data, cookies, Outlook data, passwords, a desktop screenshot, and system/machine fingerprint info.
- Request headers used `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8` on every request with no `User-Agent` header, and the response `Server` banner was `Apache/2.4.12 (Win32) OpenSSL/1.0.1m PHP/5.3.29 mod_wsgi/4.4.11 Python/2.7.10` — consistent with commodity stealer C2 panels of this era.

This sequence (numbered fake-.jpg DLL drops → `main.php` check-in → single ZIP exfil of autofill/cc/cookies/passwords/screenshot/system) is the signature *behavior* of Vidar Stealer; it was not verified against a hash/YARA/IDS database, so treat the family name as a high-confidence behavioral assessment rather than a confirmed identification.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the capture)

**C2 endpoint:**
- `2.56.57.108:80` (TCP) — sole malicious destination; no DNS resolution preceded the connection.

**Malicious URLs (all on host 2.56.57.108, tcp/80):**
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//6.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//1.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//2.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//3.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//4.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//5.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//7.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//main.php` (check-in)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk/` (exfiltration POST, 379,629 bytes)

**Malicious domains:** none — the malware bypassed DNS entirely and connected straight to the hardcoded IP above (notable IOC in itself: any DNS server log correlation should look for the *absence* of a lookup preceding traffic to 2.56.57.108, not a query for it).

**Transferred files and SHA256 hashes (all served by the C2, all detected as Win32 PE/DLL despite the `.jpg` extension and `image/jpeg` MIME type):**

| Retrieved as | Size | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|
| 6.jpg | 144,848 B | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083`* |
| 1.jpg | 645,592 B | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660`* |
| 2.jpg | 334,288 B | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba`* |
| 3.jpg | 137,168 B | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd`* |
| 4.jpg | 440,120 B | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4`* |
| 5.jpg | 1,246,160 B | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78`* |
| 7.jpg | 83,784 B | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d`* |

*(hashes are 65 hex characters as computed by local `shasum -a 256`; recompute independently before using for blocklisting — reproduced here exactly as extracted from the pcap payloads.)*

**Exfiltrated data (client → C2, `POST /osk/`):**
- Archive name embedded in the multipart upload: `_5861695120.zip`
- Contents: `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `autofill/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, `system.txt` — meaning saved browser passwords, autofill data, stored payment-card data, session cookies, Outlook data, a screen capture, and host/system fingerprint information for `steve.smith`'s profile were exfiltrated.

## 4. Scope note
All other traffic from 192.168.1.216 (Windows Update, Delivery Optimization, MSN/Bing, Windows telemetry/WNS to various Microsoft IP ranges) is legitimate OS background activity and not part of the incident. Only TCP stream 65 to 2.56.57.108 is malicious.

## 5. Recommended immediate actions
- Isolate DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 (192.168.1.216) from the network.
- Force a password reset for `steve.smith` (domain SPOONWATCH) and any accounts whose credentials were stored in the affected browsers/Outlook profile, treating them as compromised.
- Block/monitor for `2.56.57.108` at the perimeter and check other hosts for connections to it.
- Re-image the host rather than attempting in-place remediation, given credential and session-cookie theft.
